Grammar · Lesson 03

Articles a / an

Use a or an when you mean one person or thing. Listen to the first sound of the next word to choose the article.

≈ 45–55 min one thing first sound 8 interactive tasks
NoticeCompare a book and an apple.
DiscoverListen to the first sound.
BuildChoose, correct, and order chunks.
UseName and describe real objects.

Notice before the rule

Listen and compare

a book   ·   a teacher   ·   an apple   ·   an email

  • What does every phrase mean: one thing or many things?
  • Say a book and an apple slowly. Which phrase has the extra n sound?
  • Look at the sound after the article. What do apple and email have in common?

Discovery check — what sounds natural?

Tap each gap, then choose a or an

1 phone
2 office
3 student
4 address

The core meaning

A and an mean the same thing. They introduce one countable person or thing that is not yet specific.

MeaningExampleWhy?
one objecta penone pen
one persona doctorone doctor
one objectan umbrellaone umbrella
one roleShe is an engineer.one engineer

Meaning check

  • Can we say a books? No. A / an means one, so the noun is singular.
  • Can we say I am teacher? In standard English, no. A singular job normally needs a / an: I am a teacher.
  • Does a phone identify one particular phone? Not yet. It introduces any one phone.

Choose with your ears

Use a before a consonant sound: a book, a car, a teacher.

Use an before a vowel sound: an apple, an office, an idea.

The Thinking Method shortcut is simple: do not ask, “What is the first letter?” Ask, “What sound do I hear first?”

Sound can be different from spelling

  • an hour — the h is silent, so the first sound is /aʊ/.
  • a university — the word begins with a /y/ sound: “you-niversity.”
  • At A0, master the common pattern first. These examples show why listening is more reliable than looking.

Build complete noun chunks

English likes a complete chunk: article + description + noun.

a job   →   a new job
an apartment   →   an expensive apartment

The article listens to the word immediately after it. Compare a car with an old car.

Drill 6 — retrieval without choices

Say the full phrase first. Reveal only after the student answers.

1 one + orange

an orange

2 one + useful app

a useful app — useful begins with a /y/ sound.

3 one + old computer

an old computer — the article listens to old.

4 job: architect

I am an architect.

Use it in real life

Desk scan: Find five singular objects near you. Say a full phrase for each: a phone, an old notebook, a cup.
Work and people: Complete true or invented sentences: I am a/an..., My friend is a/an..., I need a/an....
Information gap: The teacher silently chooses an object. The student asks, Is it a phone? Is it an eraser? Continue until the student identifies it.
Fast fluency round: Teacher says a noun. Student immediately says the complete chunk. Use: email, client, office, meeting, hour, university, idea, problem.

Then give one example that is true about your life.
